title: Juneteenth Celebration at Academy Art Museum
author: Staff Writer
content:
Juneteenth Celebration at Academy Art Museum

 May 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 249
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Academy Art Museum will host its "13th Annual Juneteenth Celebration: Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow" on Saturday, June 22 from Noon to 4 p.m.The event is free and open to the public at the downtown Easton musuem.
The event is presented by AAM, Building African American Minds (BAAM), the Frederick Douglass Honor Society, and the Talbot County Free Library. This year's theme focuses on local fashion. Four exhibitors, Buzz Arts, Not a Phase Clothing, Black Squirrel Company, and Dinah Wilson, will showcase their unique fashions at AAM's outdoor runway. A free outdoor block party also features musical performances, a hands-on art project for families, vendors selling hand-made goods, and food vendors, as well as an exhibition of works on paper by Washington, D.C./Tilghman Island-based artist Darlene Taylor in the Museum.
New this year, the Easton museum is offering a prize-based essay contest. School-aged students from Grades 8 — 12 are invited to write essays that explore the theme: "What does Juneteenth Mean to Youth Today: Perspectives on Freedom and Equality." Winners will share their essays at the Juneteenth Celebration. Essays are due May 31.
The lead sponsor for the event is Morgan Stanley and Lisa Hunter and Shane Hatfield at the financial firm's Easton.
Additional support is being provided provided by Maryland Public Television, Bette S. Kenzie, Catherine Collins McCoy, Bay Imprint, Susan and Richard Granville and Talbot Arts.
The Juneteenth holiday celebrates when word of President Abraham Lincoln's 1863 Emancipation Proclamation reached plantations and enslaved persons across the Confederate states.
For more: https://academyartmuseum.org/

title: Ceremony honors 18 Black Union soldiers buried in Unionville cemetery
author: Tom McCall
content:
Ceremony honors 18 Black Union soldiers buried in Unionville cemetery

 May 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 618
 Words 

 Read News Document

 UNIONVILLE — It was a soulful reckoning with history.Soldiers clad in Union Army uniforms filled their barrels with gunpowder and fired three rounds to mark each of the names.
The loud volleys brought the assembled crowd to a quiet reverence.
John Blackwell …
Ennels Clayton …
Isaac Copper …
John Copper …
Eighteen names. Eighteen volleys of musket fire.
The men fought for the Union. They fought for freedom. Their freedom.
The 18 were Black Union soldiers who fought in the Civil War. They are buried in the cemetery behind St. Stephens AME Church in Unionville, the town named to honor their fight for freedom.
"Hearing the names is the best part," Pamela Roberts Price said. She has relatives in the graveyard.
Around 70 people gathered at St. Stephens on a recent Sunday. There was a contingent of Union-garbed men with rifles, flags and shiny brass buckles.
The sounds of "Amazing Grace" drifted over gravestones that are worn by thousands of rainy days. A solo violin played "Taps."
St. Stephens Pastor Eddie Scott opened the ceremony with a prayer. "Comfort us in knowing that these soldiers that we stand on their shoulders, that we can have life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness."
Harriette Lowery has more than 10 relatives in the cemetery.
"I am related to one of the soldiers, definitely," she said. "Benjamin Demby is my great-great-grandfather. My grandfather's mother was Agnes Demby Green. That was Benjamin's mother."
Like Price, Lowery loves hearing the names.
"Every time I hear the names it gives me such pride," she said. "Thinking about the chaos that is happening in our community or somewhere else, thinking about what they did, what they went through really touches me."
She noted that there were no promises to these soldiers.
"They did it hoping they would be free," Lowery said. "They hoped they would get emancipation."
She noted some of the local Black soldiers traveled as far as Texas, and some of them had to walk from Texas to get home.
"I want the history to be told over and over again because not only do our young people, all races of young people, need to know what they went through," Lowery said. "They sacrificed for us to do better. So don't give up on education and things like that. They need to know what people sacrificed."
Dan Cowgill of Middletown was master of ceremonies for the event. His ancestors were Quakers who donated the land for Unionville where freed slaves settled after the Civil War.
"We are honoring the 18 soldiers from the U.S. colored troops during the Civil War that created the town of Unionville," he said. "It is amazing I still get choked up when I read these words."
The African American history within 10 miles of St. Stephens Church is remarkable. Not all of it is known or even written about. Sandy Johnson is working to change that.
"I am a budding historic preservationist," she said. "It is good to honor those that came before us. It gives us a direction to know where we are going in life. Without the past you really can't move forward."
There were white participants in the crowd whose roots go way back too. Some of their relatives had owned big estates. Some have tilled this land for generations. A few got together to swap stories and show old black and white photographs. You could hear them saying old names too.
The Green Meadows Bluegrass Band finished playing "Amazing Grace," the sounds of the music falling softly on the worn gravestones marked with the names of the Union soldiers — John Blackwell, Ennels Clayton, Isaac Copper, John Copper, Benjamin Demby, Charles Demby, William Doane, William Doran, Horace Gibson, Zachary Glasgow, Joseph Gooby, Joseph H. Johnson, Peter Johnson, Edward Jones, Enolds Money, Frederick Pipes, Henry Roberts and Mathew Roberts.

title: Collective power in the forefront of caucus meeting
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Collective power in the forefront of caucus meeting

 June 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 697
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Civil rights activists from across the state gathered in Cambridge Thursday evening for a meeting that prominently featured calls for community activism, collective support and celebration of high-achieving students. This was the first in-person meeting the Caucus of African American Leaders has held in Cambridge in four years.Over 60 people and a half dozen Maryland political leaders attended the meeting at the Harriet Tubman Cultural and Educational Center, where they discussed the caucus' involvement around the state and in matters concerning the Eastern Shore.
Carl Snowden, convener of the caucus, spoke to the power of collective action in addressing civil rights issues. He pulled examples from history. Snowden said that the 13-month bus boycotts succeeded through collective activism, and the people were able to make sacrifices together and accomplish goals together.
Snowden spoke of the bumblebees and the hornets to drive home the point. Though the bumblebee is bigger than the hornet, the hornet is by far more feared, he said.
"There can be a thousand bumblebees, and you can kill each bumblebee one at a time, but not a single bumblebee will do a thing. They just wait their turn," Snowden said. "But if you put your hand on a hornet, every hornet in that mess will come out. They organize their collective. They understand when you touch one of us, you touch all of us."
He continued, "The purpose of the Caucus of African American leaders is to make it crystal clear that … wherever Black people are, when you go to injure one of us, you're going to have all of us to deal with."
Snowden encouraged attendees to join the Caucus of African American Leaders and be prepared to "be like hornets to deal with an issue."
In the crowd, Snowden pointed out Kionte Williams-Taylor, who Snowden said had been beaten and, as a result, hospitalized by police in a Somerset County community last Saturday. According to Snowden, the case is being reviewed by the ACLU and involves a video of the incident.
"For those of you who don't know it, we have a young man among us who was the victim of police brutality," Snowden said to attendees. "... according to what he told me, the police officer told him, 'Nobody can do anything about this. Nothing will be done.' He's about to experience what happens when hornets come together."
Robert Johnson, a representative for the campaign to elect Angela Alsobrooks, spoke of the importance of working together as a community and looking closely at the systems that make communities fight each other and divide against each other.
He urged attendees to register to vote and take the time to be politically active.
"The biggest enemy against us right now is complacency and individuals saying that it doesn't matter," Johnson said. "Do whatever it takes to get people off of the couch. And here, if they don't want to, if they're not thinking about the top of the ballot, politics of what? Local. Start local and work your way up."
Students were honored during the meeting for their academic high achievements and leadership. Those who earned recognition were Armani Black, Willoh Ryans, Aliyah Black and Tearra Brown.
Toward the end of the meeting, Carl Snowden spoke again. He expressed the importance of working together to rename the Frederick C. Malkus Bridge, which spans the Choptank River, in honor of Gloria Richardson, a civil rights activist and leader of the Cambridge Movement.
Snowden stressed the importance of not waiting around for an official change by the government and that the collective power of the Black community has the power to effect change regardless of official documents. Snowden said about 50 years ago, in Washington, D.C., Black people decided to honor Malcolm X, an American revolutionary and human rights activist, by renaming Meridian Park after Malcolm X.
"Now, the government did not officially change it," Snowden said. "The government didn't pass any resolution. The government didn't approve it. But Black people said, 'We want to remember Malcolm X,' and they named Meridian Park after Malcolm X. Well, I would request those of you here, when you cross the bridge and go into the bridge, just tell people you are going into the Gloria Richardson Bridge."

title: 4th annual Caroline Pride Fest Draws hundreds
author: Tom McCall
content:
4th annual Caroline Pride Fest Draws hundreds

 June 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 491
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — A crowd of around 1,000 came to Denton for the fourth annual Caroline Pride Festival on Saturday. This family-friendly event had live music, drag queens, belly dancers, funnel cakes and 85 vendors, which filled Market Street.The festival received a proclamation from the Town of Denton that claimed June 1 as Pride Day. It said, in part, that Caroline County is a place that strives for inclusion and welcomes everybody.
The motto of the festival was "Diversity Creates Community."
Angel Perez, the founder of the festival, said, "Pride represents an opportunity to raise awareness about diversity, inclusion and respect and the importance of a society based in equity. Pride Month reminds us we need to continue to fight for our rights to be included, to feel welcome and be respected as a human being."
After marking the significance of the 1969 Stonewall Riots, which many see as the beginning of LGBTQ+ movement, he continued.
"We need to continue to educate our community, because a community where there are no labels, where each person respects their neighbors regardless of sexual orientation, will be a strong, united and thriving community. Together we can achieve it," Perez said.
He guessed that 500 people were milling around the vendors and the stage area. He expected around 1,000 visitors for the whole day.
Perez wanted to emphasize the events's growth over the past few years.
"Our first year, we had 40 vendors. This year we have more than 85 vendors. The festival also serves to raise awareness and educate our community," Perez said.
Davina Reign Escade, the reigning 2024 Miss Trans Maryland, took the stage and introduced Lt. Gov. Aruna Miller.
"We are going to build a state where no one gets left behind. What that means is that we want to make sure that every individual in the state of Maryland can live their authentic lives. They can love who they want to love, because love is love, right?" Miller said.
Before taking the stage, Escade got a chance to talk with Miller for about 45 minutes.
"She invited me and the rest of the board of directors of Caroline Pride to take some students from the high schools and bring them over to meet the Governor and get their opinion on what they think they need in their community," Escade said.
She had a few ideas she said could improve the lives of youths in the LGBTQ+ community.
"I want to see more sensitivity training in our schools. And I would love to see more HIV care out there on the Eastern Shore. There is not a lot," Escade said. "When I was 15, I contracted HIV. I have lived with it for almost 15 years now. It is very important that these kids know that there is someone to guide them. They are going to be ok. HIV positive is not a death sentence anymore. I am 15 years positive and I am thriving and healthy and beautiful. I am doing cartwheels at Pride."

title: Gunsallus, Montgomery face wrath of residents
author: Jim Johnson jjohnson@chespub.com
content:
Gunsallus, Montgomery face wrath of residents

 June 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Jim Johnson jjohnson@chespub.com | Section: Columns 
 
 686
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Easton Town Council President Frank Gunsallus and council member David Montgomery are consistent.In January, the two council members voted against a public assembly permit for the Delmarva Pride Center's annual Pride festival planned for June 13 to 16.
Then at the May 20 council meeting, Gunsallus suggested that town funds not be used to fund Pride flags and banners.
Gunsallus called the Pride flag "antithetical to America."
"I believe that it is a socialist endeavor parading beyond or behind the guise of a social movement," Gunsallus said May 20. "And I think that we should not be using taxpayer funds to support a cause that is antithetical to our country and our principles and our Constitution."
Montgomery was the only one on the council to voice support at the May meeting and again at the June 3 meeting for Gunsallus' position.
The council chambers were packed June 3 with residents, most voicing opposition to Gunsallus' statements but a few supporting the council president.
After listening to the comments, Gunsallus made a short statement.
"I'd like to clear the air — the absolute truth is that I firmly believe all people are equal and should be treated as such," he said. "This is why I support every member of our community."
He said his aim was fiscal responsibility, not bigotry toward the LGBTQ+ community.
"While aiming to be cognizant of the challenges they face, as an elected official, I must be fiscally responsible and use hard-earned taxpayer dollars to support the town's operational needs. And that was the focus of my comments from the last meeting. I apologize if my intent was not clear."
Gunsallus drew support from Montgomery. The councilman supported Gunsallus' statements about the flags on May 20, and he doubled down Monday evening.
"We were discussing first an issue about the town displaying Pride flags," Montgomery said. "… I do not believe it is the town's business to make everyone feel good about their identity."
Montgomery continued, stating the country is being "torn apart by identity politics." He called out the transgender community's involvement in the LGBTQ+ movement specifically.
"This is about the hijacking of the movement by a transexual ideology," he said.
"I've listened to everyone here, and I've noticed that every one of you misstated what Frank and I were talking about," Montgomery said, referencing the May 20 comments. "What I stated was that there is a danger to our community from promotion of this transexual ideology.
"... This town has no business putting up flags that promote the notion that you will feel better, you will solve your teenage problems if you decide that you should go out and demand your sex be changed," he continued. "That's what I object to, nothing about any individual."
Gunsallus and Montgomery were alone in their views on the council.
Mayor Megan Cook summed up the views of the other three council members, denouncing Gunsallus' original comments.
"I feel those comments were dangerous, and they do foster a climate of intolerance and exclusion," Cook said. "Asserting that the Pride flag or support of our LGBTQ community is antithetical to our country or our Constitution is incorrect."
The mayor sees damage to Easton when such comments are made by elected officials.
"When such divisive comments are made, it begins to tear at the fabric of our town."
Gunsallus and Montgomery are consistent in their opposition to Pride events and recognition in Easton. They voted against a permit for the Pride festival, and now they are challenging the display of flags and banners in the town.
That is their right. They were elected to the council, and they need to vote for what they believe is in the best interest of Easton. They should not, however, expect to voice such opinions without drawing vehement opposition as they did last week.
Flags and banners are displayed throughout the year. The town should support a wide range of people, lifestyles and viewpoints. The Pride festival deserves Easton's support as it strives to be an inclusive, welcoming community.
The Rev. Elmer Davis Jr. is a voice of reason on the council. Gunsallus and Montgomery should heed his words.
"We should learn to love everybody," Davis said. "We're not all going to agree on things."
